p: The video starts with text posing the problem of multiple document versions in Slack. It shows an online doc where a user leaves an inline comment requesting a cut from 6 weeks to 3 weeks. A terminal command demonstrates Claude editing the doc based on the comment and republishing to the same URL. The doc updates with the resolved thread, ending on an Artifact Share call to action.
Artifact Share lets teams comment directly on docs generated by AI, allowing the AI to update the existing URL without link proliferation.

[{"timestamp":"00:00","observation":"Text hook addressing Slack doc version confusion over a blurred interface."},{"timestamp":"00:06","observation":"Zoom-in to highlight text and leave an inline review comment."},{"timestamp":"00:11","observation":"Terminal prompt triggers Claude to update the doc from comments."},{"timestamp":"00:17","observation":"The document refreshes to show the updated scope with the thread resolved."},{"timestamp":"00:23","observation":"Final CTA text screen showing value proposition and website URL."}]

The video presents a clear workflow that solves the stated version control problem. UI captures are legible and pacing matches each beat well. Audio presence is minimal, but the visual progression communicates the core concept effectively.

p: ["hook does not match creative brief's 'versions in Slack' concept — no Slack UI or version-confusion visual at all","opening frame is a static decision-doc screenshot, low pattern-interrupt for a scrolling dev feed","product branding (Artifact Share name/URL) only appears in the final ~1 second; most runtime is spent on the doc mockup and a generic terminal, not the product's own UI"]

The sequence (comment on doc → claude -p apply → republished v2 → tagline) does land the intended message of 'humans point, agents edit, same URL,' and the CLI-to-republish beat is a clean, legible demonstration of the mechanic. But the actual footage abandons the stated hook entirely — there's no Slack, no '10 versions, which is latest' confusion — so it can't be judged as executing that concept, and a plain business-doc screenshot is a weak scroll-stopper for a dev audience. Visual execution is clean and text is crisp throughout, but product identity is thin until the last frame.
